subtitle: Wrap every API error in the same shape, so clients always know where to look.
notes: This deck goes with exercise 11. By the end you should be able to explain what an exception handler does and turn any DRF error into one standard JSON shape.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.text:
Things go wrong in every API: a missing field, a task that doesn't exist, a user who isn't logged in. The server still answers, with a **status code** like `404` and a JSON body.

DRF's default error bodies come in **different shapes**. Your **exception handler** is a help desk that files every complaint on the **same form**.
slides.notes: You've met exceptions in data analysis: a typo in df["prise"] raises KeyError. DRF has its own exceptions for web errors, like NotFound, and calls a handler function to turn them into responses.

slides.title: What your code receives
slides.caption: The tests pass an exception in as `exc`, and an empty dict `{}` as `context`.
slides.code:
from rest_framework import exceptions

# test 2 does this:
response = api_exception_handler(exceptions.NotFound(), {})

# other exceptions the tests pass in as exc:
exceptions.ValidationError({"title": ["This field is required."]})
exceptions.NotAuthenticated()       # 401
exceptions.MethodNotAllowed("POST") # 405
KeyError("boom")                    # a bug, not a web error
slides.notes: You never create these yourself inside the function. exc and response only exist while a test is calling your function. context normally says which view failed; you just pass it along.

slides.title: Two shapes in, one shape out
slides.caption: Same status code, but every body gets the `"error"` envelope.
slides.notes: Validation errors are keyed by field name. Every other error has one "detail" key. That difference is why you need an if.

terms.meaning: A function that turns an exception into a response. DRF calls it.
`400` bad input, `401` not logged in, `403` not allowed, `404` not found.
A server bug. Unexpected errors should stay 500s.
"The data you sent is wrong", with messages per field.
A fixed outer shape around every body, like `{"error": {...}}`.

slides.title: Tool: DRF's exception_handler
slides.caption: Already called on the first line of your function. A bug gives back `None`.
slides.code:
from rest_framework import exceptions
from rest_framework.views import exception_handler
response = exception_handler(exceptions.NotFound(), {})
print(response.status_code)
print(response.data)
print(exception_handler(KeyError("oops"), {}))    # a bug, not a web error
slides.notes: ErrorDetail is DRF's special string that also remembers an error code. It behaves like normal text, and str() turns it into a plain string.

slides.title: Tools: str and isinstance
slides.code:
from rest_framework import exceptions
from rest_framework.views import exception_handler

response = exception_handler(exceptions.ParseError(), {})
print(str(response.data["detail"]))      # plain text

# isinstance asks: "is this value that kind of thing?"
bad = exceptions.ValidationError("bad")
print(isinstance(bad, exceptions.ValidationError))
print(isinstance(exceptions.NotFound(), exceptions.ValidationError))
slides.notes: str(...) turns an ErrorDetail into plain text. isinstance gives True or False. In your file ValidationError is already imported by name, so you can write isinstance(exc, ValidationError). Check for None with `is None`, not == None.

slides.title: Dots vs square brackets
slides.notes: response["status_code"] doesn't work, and neither does response.data.detail. The object uses dots; the dict inside it uses brackets. You can also replace the whole dict: response.data = {...}.

slides.title: Pattern: choose, then wrap
slides.caption: The same shape your handler needs, on different data:
slides.notes: First pick the two changing values with if / else, then build the nested dict once. A dict inside a dict is just a value that happens to be a dict.

steps.text: Keep the first line; if `response` is `None`, return `None`

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Reading `["detail"]` on a validation error: `KeyError`. Check it first
Returning your dict instead of `response`: the tests need `.status_code`
Typing `"status": 400` by hand: test 5 checks 405, 429 and 400
Turning `None` into a response: real bugs should stay 500s

slides.title: Where you'll use this
slides.text: A React app shows a red banner whenever an API call fails. With one error shape, it only needs `body["error"]["message"]`, whatever went wrong.
bullets: Switch it on once, with the `EXCEPTION_HANDLER` setting
Mobile apps and other services get the same predictable errors
Unexpected bugs still become 500s, which you log and fix
slides.notes: The setting is REST_FRAMEWORK = {"EXCEPTION_HANDLER": "core.exceptions.api_exception_handler"}. Every view in the project then uses your handler.

slides.title: Check yourself
questions: What does `exception_handler` give back for a `KeyError`, and why?
Why must you check for `ValidationError` before reading `"detail"`?
Why use `response.status_code` instead of typing the number?
Why return `response`, not the dictionary you built?
